title: Trapping Rain Water II
description: Brute force to optimized: repeated relaxation until convergence versus a min-heap-driven, Dijkstra-like expansion from the grid's border.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given an m x n integer matrix heightMap representing the height of each unit cell in a 2D elevation map, return the total volume of water it can trap after raining.

blocks.caption: Border cells start as the initial "walls"; a min-heap always expands inward from the lowest wall found

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","An m x n integer matrix heightMap"],["Output","The total volume of water trapped after raining, treating the matrix as a 3D elevation surface"],["Goal","Find this efficiently, generalizing the classic 1D \"Trapping Rain Water\" problem to two dimensions"],["Constraints","m == heightMap.length; n == heightMap[i].length; 1 <= m, n <= 200; 0 <= heightMap[i][j] <= 2 * 10^4"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["Water can only be trapped if it's enclosed by walls on ALL SIDES (not just left/right as in the 1D version)","The border of the grid is the only place water can ever escape, making every border cell an initial \"wall\" of its own height"],["The amount trapped at any interior cell depends on the LOWEST surrounding barrier that still encloses it","Always process the current globally lowest known wall first, a classic min-heap driven, Dijkstra-like expansion"],["Once water is trapped at a cell, that cell effectively becomes part of the wall for whatever is beyond it","When a cell is processed, \"push it back\" into consideration with an effective height of max(current wall, its own height), extending the wall inward"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Given a 2D elevation map, compute how much water would be trapped after rain, where water can only be trapped if it's enclosed on every side by higher (or equal) terrain, with the grid's outer border acting as the only place water can drain away.

blocks.title: Analogy: Flooding a Terrain From Its Lowest Border Point Inward
blocks.text: Like slowly flooding a bowl-shaped terrain by always breaching its CURRENT lowest boundary point first (since water always finds the lowest escape route), and letting water spread inward from there. Every newly flooded interior point either lets water through freely (if it's already tall enough) or gets partially submerged (trapping water up to the height of the lowest boundary point that let the flood reach it); either way, that point now becomes part of the boundary going forward.

blocks.caption: Popping the lowest wall and pushing discovered neighbors back with a raised effective height

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: A 5x5 bowl-shaped elevation (border height 3, ring height 2, center height 1)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The 8 cells forming the inner ring (height 2) are each enclosed by the border (height 3)","Each ring cell traps 3 - 2 = 1 unit","8 ring cells contribute 8 * 1 = 8 units total"],["The single center cell (height 1) is enclosed by the ring, whose effective wall height (after being raised) is 3","The center cell traps 3 - 1 = 2 units","The ring, once \"flooded\" to height 3, becomes the effective boundary for the center"],["Answer","10","8 (ring) + 2 (center) = 10 total units of trapped water"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: grid smaller than 3x3 in either dimension
If the grid has fewer than 3 rows or fewer than 3 columns, there can be no interior cell fully enclosed on all sides, so no water can ever be trapped, and the answer is 0.
5. How Should We Think?

Before trying to relax every cell repeatedly against its neighbors until some fixed point is reached, notice that always expanding from the GLOBALLY lowest known boundary first guarantees each cell's true trapped water level is determined the first time it's reached.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Water can only ever be trapped if it's enclosed by terrain reaching the grid's border on every side, so every border cell is, by definition, already at the "water surface" level (height equal to its own terrain), and no water is trapped there.

Observation 2: Starting with all border cells in a min-heap (ordered by height), the LOWEST wall in the entire current boundary is always processed first, since it represents the point where water would first overflow or be constrained.

Observation 3: When the lowest wall cell is popped and an unvisited interior neighbor is examined, that neighbor traps water up to the popped cell's height if the neighbor is shorter (max(0, wallHeight - neighborHeight)); the neighbor itself now becomes part of the boundary going forward, with an EFFECTIVE height of max(wallHeight, neighborHeight) (its own height if taller, or the water's surface level if it was shorter).

Observation 4: Repeating this process (always popping the currently lowest boundary cell, computing trapped water at each newly discovered neighbor, and pushing that neighbor back with its raised effective height) until every cell has been visited exactly once, correctly computes the total trapped volume.

Recognizing that processing cells in strictly increasing order of their EFFECTIVE boundary height (via a min-heap) guarantees each cell's trapped water is correctly and finally determined the moment it's first reached is the key structural insight, directly analogous to Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm's greedy, priority-ordered expansion.

This is a min-heap-driven, Dijkstra-like expansion pattern: always process the globally lowest known boundary cell next, computing trapped water and extending the effective boundary inward as the search proceeds.
6. Brute Force Solution

Repeatedly relax every interior cell's water level against its 4 neighbors until no cell's level can be lowered any further (a fixed-point iteration), analogous to Bellman-Ford's repeated edge relaxation instead of Dijkstra's single-pass, priority-ordered approach.
Step by step algorithm

items: Initialize every border cell's water level to its own height (border cells never trap water), and every interior cell's water level to a very large placeholder value.

Repeatedly scan all interior cells, lowering a cell's water level to the maximum of its own terrain height and the MINIMUM water level among its 4 neighbors, whenever this would decrease its current level; repeat until a full pass makes no changes at all.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Border cells are initialized directly to their own height, since they can never trap any water regardless of the surrounding terrain.
Interior cells start at a very large placeholder value, representing "not yet determined", and are only ever lowered, never raised, as relaxation proceeds.
The outer while loop repeats until an entire pass produces no changes, guaranteeing every cell has reached its final, correct water level.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Repeated relaxation eventually converges to the correct water level for every cell, so the final total is always accurate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O((rows * cols) squared) in the worst case, since a full relaxation pass can be needed up to O(rows*cols) times before convergence.
Space: O(rows * cols) for the water-level grid.

Limitation: repeatedly re-scanning and relaxing every interior cell, potentially many times over, ignores that processing cells in strictly increasing order of boundary height (via a min-heap) can determine each cell's final water level in a single, one-shot pass, exactly analogous to why Dijkstra's algorithm outperforms repeated Bellman-Ford-style relaxation.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force repeatedly relaxes every cell until convergence. Instead, use a min-heap seeded with every border cell (at its own height), and expand strictly in order of increasing height, exactly like Dijkstra's algorithm. Popping the lowest current boundary cell and examining its unvisited neighbors determines each neighbor's trapped water IMMEDIATELY and CORRECTLY (never needing revision later), since no cell processed afterward could ever present a lower effective boundary than what has already been established. Push each newly discovered neighbor back into the heap with its raised effective height, extending the boundary inward one cell at a time.

Seed a min-heap with every border cell (height, row, col), marking them all visited. While the heap is non-empty, pop the lowest-height cell; for each of its unvisited neighbors, add max(0, poppedHeight - neighborHeight) to the total trapped water, mark the neighbor visited, and push it back with height max(poppedHeight, neighborHeight). Return the accumulated total once the heap empties.
9. Optimized Solution
Use a min-heap to always expand from the currently lowest boundary cell, computing and accumulating trapped water at each newly discovered neighbor.
Dry run for a 5x5 bowl (border height 3, ring height 2, center height 1)

blocks.content: {"headers":["Popped wall (height)","Newly discovered neighbor(s)","Water added","Running total"],"rows":[["Border cell, h=3","One ring cell, h=2","3-2=1","1"],["Border cell, h=3","One ring cell, h=2","3-2=1","2"],["Ring cell (now h=3), h=3","One ring cell, h=2","3-2=1","3"],["Ring cell (now h=3), h=3","Center cell, h=1, AND one ring cell, h=2","(3-1)+(3-2)=2+1=3","6"],["Ring cell (now h=3), h=3","One ring cell, h=2","3-2=1","7"],["Ring cell (now h=3), h=3","One ring cell, h=2","3-2=1","8"],["Ring cell (now h=3), h=3","One ring cell, h=2","3-2=1","9"],["Ring cell (now h=3), h=3","One ring cell, h=2","3-2=1","10"]]}

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The 8 ring cells each contribute 1 unit (8 total), and the single center cell contributes 2 units, giving a final total of 10, matching the expected answer.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows * cols * log(rows * cols)), since every cell is pushed and popped from the heap at most once, each operation costing O(log(rows*cols)).
Space: O(rows * cols) for the visited grid and the heap.
Why This Works

Processing cells in strictly increasing order of their (possibly raised) effective height guarantees that when a cell is popped, every cell that could ever constrain its trapped water level from a LOWER height has already been considered; no cell processed later could ever present a lower boundary. This means the water level computed for a newly discovered neighbor at the moment of its discovery is final and correct, exactly mirroring why Dijkstra's algorithm never needs to revisit or revise a node's shortest distance once it has been finalized.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["A newly discovered neighbor is shorter than the popped wall","It traps water equal to the difference, and is pushed back with the WALL's (raised) height as its new effective boundary height"],["A newly discovered neighbor is taller than or equal to the popped wall","It traps no water, and is pushed back with its OWN height, since it now forms a taller part of the boundary"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: Every border cell is seeded into the heap and marked visited upfront, since border cells can never trap water and always define the initial escape boundary.
The min-heap ensures cells are always processed in strictly increasing order of their current effective height, mirroring Dijkstra's priority queue.

max(currentHeight, neighborHeight) correctly computes the neighbor's EFFECTIVE height for future processing, whether it was submerged (raised to the wall's level) or already tall enough (using its own height).

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (repeated relaxation until convergence)","O((rows * cols) squared)","O(rows * cols)","Analogous to Bellman-Ford's repeated edge relaxation"],["Optimized (min-heap, Dijkstra-like expansion)","O(rows * cols * log(rows * cols))","O(rows * cols)","Each cell's final water level is determined in a single pass, never revised"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

This problem is a direct 2D generalization of the classic 1D "Trapping Rain Water" problem, solved with a min-heap-driven expansion strategy directly analogous to Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm: always expand from the currently lowest known boundary, finalizing each cell's value the moment it's first reached.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to seed ALL border cells into the heap upfront, which would incorrectly allow water to seem trapped along parts of the border that should actually be free-draining.
Pushing a discovered neighbor back with its OWN height always, instead of max(current wall height, its own height), which would incorrectly lower the effective boundary for cells beyond it.

Using a max-heap or unordered processing instead of a min-heap, which would break the crucial "always expand from the lowest boundary first" guarantee that makes each cell's final value correct on first visit.

blocks.text: Edge cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["Grid has fewer than 3 rows or 3 columns","No interior cell can be fully enclosed, so the answer is 0"],["The entire grid is flat (all the same height)","No water is trapped anywhere, since no cell is lower than its surrounding boundary"],["The grid has a very tall single spike surrounded by a bowl","Correctly handled, since the spike is simply never shorter than any wall reaching it, so it contributes no trapped water at its own position, while cells around it still trap correctly"]]}

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Explicitly connect this problem to Dijkstra's algorithm (both always expand from the globally lowest/shortest known frontier first), since recognizing this structural analogy demonstrates a much deeper understanding than just memorizing "use a min-heap here".

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Trapping rain water, but in a 2D grid (not a 1D array)" points toward a min-heap-driven expansion starting from the grid's border, directly analogous to Dijkstra's algorithm, rather than the simpler two-pointer technique used in the classic 1D version.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How does this relate to the classic 1D Trapping Rain Water problem? That problem uses a simpler two-pointer technique since water can only escape from exactly 2 directions (left and right); this 2D version needs the full min-heap/Dijkstra-like approach since water can escape through any point on the entire border.

How would you also report exactly where the trapped water sits (a full water-level map, not just the total volume)? Track the computed effective height at each cell as it's finalized, storing max(0, effectiveHeight - originalHeight) per cell instead of just accumulating a running sum.

What if the grid had "holes" (missing/undefined cells) partway through? This would require treating those cells as additional border-like escape points, seeding them into the initial heap alongside the true border cells.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: A direct 2D generalization of the classic 1D Trapping Rain Water problem, using a min-heap-driven expansion strategy structurally identical to Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O((rows * cols) squared) time, O(rows * cols) space.
Optimized (min-heap, Dijkstra-like expansion): O(rows * cols * log(rows * cols)) time, O(rows * cols) space.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Min-heap-driven expansion from the grid's border, directly analogous to Dijkstra's shortest-path algorithm
Core Idea: Always process the currently lowest known boundary cell first; every newly discovered neighbor's trapped water is finalized correctly the moment it's first reached
Time: O(rows * cols * log(rows * cols))
Space: O(rows * cols)

Most Important Observation: Processing cells in strictly increasing order of effective boundary height guarantees each cell's trapped water is determined correctly on first visit, never needing revision
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Seed the border into a min-heap; pop the lowest wall, trap water at new neighbors, push them back raised to max(wall, self)
